assertions.text: Fulfillment method splitting is represented as its own table — items with different fulfillment types (store pickup vs home delivery) cannot share a shipment.
assertions.evidence: Fulfillment method splitting is combined with delivery address and availability splitting in Table 1 (Shipment Grouping), not in its own dedicated table.

assertions.text: Delivery address splitting is represented as its own table — items going to different addresses must be in separate shipments.
assertions.evidence: Delivery address splitting is combined with fulfillment method and availability in Table 1, not in its own dedicated table.

assertions.text: Availability splitting is represented as its own table — in-stock items ship immediately, backordered/pre-ordered items ship when available.
assertions.evidence: Availability splitting is combined with fulfillment and address splitting in Table 1, not in its own dedicated table.

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation (minimising shipments) is represented as its own table — choosing which warehouses to ship from to minimise total shipment count.
assertions.evidence: Table 2 (Warehouse Allocation) is dedicated entirely to this concern, with scenarios covering single warehouse, multi-warehouse splits, and insufficient stock.

assertions.text: Companion product grouping is represented as its own table — paired items (e.g. camera body and lens) should ship together from the same location when possible.
assertions.evidence: Table 3 (Companion Product Co-shipment) is dedicated entirely to this concern with five scenarios.

assertions.text: Fulfillment table covers at least: all items for home delivery, all items for store pickup, and a mix of delivery and pickup items.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 shows: 'All items identical' (home delivery), 'Two pickup items at same store' (all pickup), and 'Home delivery alongside store pickup' (mix).

assertions.text: Delivery address table covers at least: all items to the same address, and items to different addresses.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 includes 'All items identical attributes' (same address) and 'Personal item and gift to different address' (different addresses).

assertions.text: Availability table covers at least: all items in stock, a mix of in-stock and pre-order/backorder, and two backordered/pre-ordered items with different dates. Pre-order and backorder are recognised as equivalent for splitting semantics.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 shows all in-stock (row 1), in-stock with pre-order (row 4), in-stock with backorder (row 5), and pre-order with backorder (row 9). Rows 4-5 treat both as equivalent (both split into 2 shipments).

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table covers at least: single warehouse has full quantity, multi-warehouse split needed, fewer-warehouse split preferred over more warehouses, and cannot fulfill (insufficient total stock).
assertions.evidence: Table 2 covers: 'One warehouse has sufficient stock' (single), 'No single warehouse covers quantity' (multi-warehouse split), 'Stock split across five...Philadelphia + Washington' (fewer preferred), 'Total stock falls short' (cannot fulfill).

assertions.text: Companion table covers at least: single warehouse has both companions, unavoidable split (no warehouse has both but both are available), and fulfillment not possible (one companion not available anywhere).
assertions.evidence: Table 3 covers shared location (row 1) and unavoidable split (row 4), but lacks a scenario where one companion is unavailable anywhere; row 5 shows both items available despite conflict.

assertions.text: Scenario names describe the business situation (e.g. 'Consolidate: two beats three', 'Everything at one warehouse') — not 'Test case 2'.
assertions.evidence: All scenarios use descriptive business language: 'Home delivery alongside store pickup', 'Stock split across five warehouses; balanced pair available', 'No shared location exists'.

assertions.text: Trigger tables represent multi-item orders where each item has its own fulfillment type, address, and availability. The notation makes the item-to-property mapping unambiguous.
assertions.evidence: Example from row 2: 'Shirt (home delivery, 123 Main St, in stock) + tripod (store pickup, Downtown, in stock)' — each item clearly mapped to its properties, not ambiguous value sets.

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table uses a scalar count column (e.g. 'Qty ordered') not item lists, when product identity doesn't matter for the logic.
assertions.evidence: Table 2 uses 'Units Needed' column with scalars (3, 6, 5, 10) and 'Warehouse Stock' with quantity pairs (Chicago: 6, LA: 2), not item lists.

assertions.text: Column names use business/domain language (e.g. 'Shipments?' not 'Result?', 'Warehouse stock' not 'inventory_map'). Tables read as specification a product person could review.
assertions.evidence: Column names include 'Shipments?', 'Warehouse Stock', 'Sub-shipments?', 'Ship Together?', 'Warehouses Selected?' — all business terminology.

assertions.text: Output/expected columns end with '?' (e.g. 'Shipments?', 'Groups?') to distinguish them from input columns.
assertions.evidence: All output columns end with '?': 'Shipments?', 'Groups?', 'Warehouses Selected?', 'Sub-shipments?', 'Ship Together?', 'Resolution?'.

assertions.text: Inventory assignments are physically valid: items are only assigned to locations that have them. Shipment counts match the assignments shown.
assertions.evidence: Table 2 row 3: '6 units needed, Chicago: 4, LA: 3' assigned to 'Chicago + LA' gives 7 total (sufficient); row 4 'Philadelphia: 3, Washington: 3' gives 6 total (exact match).

assertions.text: Multiple open questions are surfaced across the tables — ambiguities, edge cases, or product decisions that the requirements don't fully specify.
assertions.evidence: Tables include: row 9 open question on pre-order/backorder grouping by date, Table 2 open questions on insufficient inventory, warehouse tiebreaker, and Table 3 open questions on forced splits and companion constraint priority.

assertions.text: Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 combines three distinct concerns (fulfillment method splitting, delivery address splitting, availability splitting) into one table, violating the principle that each concern should be separately addressable.

assertions.text: Each table has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns. Fewer rows per table is expected when concerns are properly separated.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 contains combinatorial rows like row 8 ('Two addresses plus a pre-order') testing multiple concerns together; row 7 ('Two pickup items at different stores') duplicates address-splitting logic from row 3 for a different fulfillment method.
